content:
A cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing a woman's husband, and she is now suing Amazon, the cargo airline 21 Air, the aircraft lessor, and the two pilots who were flying the plane at the time for wrongful death.

The plaintiff, Yaraisi Santiso Morejon, filed the lawsuit in Miami-Dade County on Wednesday, alleging multiple failures led to the death of her 53-year-old husband, Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo. Rodriguez was one of the five people killed when Amazon Air Flight 7598 overran the runway and struck a passenger van carrying a cleaning crew who were finishing up their last job before heading home.

Jorge Garcia, a lawyer at Morgan & Morgan who is representing Santiso, said: "This is a very hardworking family that came to the United States from Cuba in 2011. They held multiple jobs and truly put down roots in the community. They are a very strong family."

Garcia noted that Rodriguez died instantly on impact. He is survived by his wife and their 22-year-old son, Ronaldo. The lawyer said Amazon has not yet contacted the family, though the company told HuffPost it is working to obtain contact information for the families of those affected.

Amazon also provided HuffPost with a statement from spokesperson Kelly Nantel issued on Tuesday, expressing condolences to the families of the deceased and stating that Amazon plans to fully cooperate with all relevant accident investigations.

Attorney Mike Morgan said: "We believe, based on the information available to us so far, this was a preventable tragedy, so filing this lawsuit now to preserve the rights of Mr. Rodriguez's estate and to preserve any relevant evidence during the NTSB investigation is very important."

Other deceased victims include 55-year-old Rolando Aleman Leon, 75-year-old Julio C. Pineda, 53-year-old Carlos Acosta Fajardo, and 47-year-old Javierkys Reyes Quevedo. NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy described the scene as "complete destruction," with the passenger van "torn apart."

The Boeing 767-300 cargo plane crash triggered a major fire and left five others seriously injured, including the two pilots, who have since been discharged from hospital. In interviews with reporters, Garcia and Morgan raised questions about the training and competence of Captain Joseph Carroll and First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina.

Morgan said: "What we have heard from the cockpit so far is nothing but chaos. We learned this morning that the throttles were still at full power 15 seconds before impact. That tells us the crew had no unified strategy, did not declare an emergency, and raises serious questions about what exactly was happening in the cockpit."

The NTSB opened its crash investigation this week, with investigators examining the aircraft in question on Tuesday. The lawyers pointed out that aircraft operator 21 Air had previously received a series of safety complaints from senior staff, and argued that Amazon either knew or should have known about the safety deficiencies involved.

The complaint states: "This catastrophe was not an unavoidable accident, but a foreseeable and preventable consequence of multiple concurrent failures." These include: "the pilots (Carroll and Molina) attempting a high-speed landing in strong tailwind conditions without executing the mandatory go-around procedure; systemic failures by defendants Amazon and 21 Air in ensuring the pilots received adequate training, maintained good health, and made proper aeronautical decisions; and the deployment by the relevant defendants of a 32-year-old aircraft whose braking, thrust reverser, and spoiler systems are currently under NTSB investigation."

The complaint further states: "Any one of the above failures would, on its own, have been sufficient to cause death; taken together, they produced a catastrophic outcome."
